title: Do good, avoid evil (ST I-II.94.2)
hook: the first principle of the natural law

segments.voice: Yesterday, what law is: an ordinance of reason for the common good, made by the one who cares for the community, and made known. Your line was reason for the common good. Which rule did you ask about? Day one thousand one hundred seventy-five.

Two sisters at a kitchen table are arguing about whether to tell their cousin the hard truth about her new boyfriend. One says tell her now. The other says wait, it isn't our place. It gets heated. They disagree about nearly everything in the conversation. But underneath the argument sits one thing neither of them says out loud, because neither needs to: both are trying to find the good thing to do. Nobody at that table is arguing for the bad option. Thomas Aquinas would call that buried agreement the first principle at work.
screen: `AN ARGUMENT AT THE KITCHEN TABLE.` → `THEY DISAGREE ABOUT NEARLY EVERYTHING.` → `BOTH WANT THE GOOD THING.`

segments.voice: Yesterday Thomas said the natural law is made known in human minds. Today he says what it starts from. He compares two kinds of thinking. When we think about what is, the first rule is that a thing can't both be and not be at the same time. Every other argument leans on that. When we think about what to do, there has to be a first rule too. And Thomas finds it in the meaning of the word good. Good is what things seek. So the first principle of the practical mind is this: good is to be done and pursued, and evil is to be avoided. Do good, avoid evil. It sounds almost too simple. That's the point. It isn't a conclusion you argue your way to; Thomas says it's known in itself, like knowing a whole is bigger than its part. And everything else in the natural law hangs from it. Then Thomas shows how it unfolds, by looking at what people are drawn to by nature. Like everything that exists, we're drawn to keep on living. Like the animals, we're drawn to bring up our young. And as reasoning creatures, we're drawn to know the truth about God and to live with others in society. So the natural law says: protect life, care for children, shun ignorance, and don't harm the people you live among. Elsewhere Thomas leans on a line from the Psalms, in the Douay-Rheims: "The light of thy countenance O Lord, is signed upon us." He reads it as the light of reason, stamped on us like a seal. Paul says something close about people without the written law: they "shew the work of the law written in their hearts." For Thomas, the moral life doesn't start with a rulebook. It starts with a light already on.
screen: `THINKING ABOUT WHAT IS, AND WHAT TO DO.` · `GOOD IS WHAT THINGS SEEK.` · `LIFE, CHILDREN, TRUTH, LIVING TOGETHER.` · `A LIGHT STAMPED ON US.` · then, large: `DO GOOD, AVOID EVIL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: do one good, avoid one evil. Settle, and breathe. Look ahead at the rest of today. Find one specific good you could do: a call you've been putting off, a dish you could wash for someone, a thank-you you owe. Make it small and real. Then find one specific harm you could steer around: a sharp comment that's been forming, a shortcut that isn't honest, a bit of gossip. Hold both in mind, side by side. If you pray, you can ask for help with each. Then let the rest go quiet. The bell holds the time.
Do good. The start of Thomas's first principle of the natural law: good is to be done and pursued, and evil avoided. Everything else hangs from it. Today's word.
Your line: the first principle. Today, when you're stuck on a choice, go back to the first question under it: which way is the good? Day one thousand one hundred seventy-five.

howItsDone: Catholic moral teaching speaks of a natural law that human reason can know, and the Catechism, drawing on Thomas, describes it as the light of understanding placed in us by God.

notes: All Aquinas is paraphrased. Check: the parallel between the first indemonstrable principle of speculative reason (non-contradiction) and of practical reason, founded on the notion of good, 'that which all things seek'; 'good is to be done and pursued, and evil is to be avoided'; self-evident, with the whole-greater-than-part example; the order of natural inclinations (self-preservation, what nature teaches all animals, knowing the truth about God and living in society) (I-II.94.2).
Psalm 4:7 as the light of natural reason, the imprint of the divine light, is from I-II.91.2; confirm the attribution.
Douay-Rheims wording and verse numbering to confirm: Psalm 4:7 and Romans 2:15 (fragment).
howItsDone paraphrases CCC 1954–1955, which quotes Thomas on the natural law as the light of understanding placed in us by God; confirm.
